and a unit-of-work class, and those usually miss the goal, because
already is a unit of work with repositories, and a generic wrapper either leaks
or hides the queries you need. Choose on purpose: use the context directly where depending on EF Core is acceptable, or write a specific repository per aggregate whose methods name the queries.
A new service starts from a popular template: Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Api projects, a
class with a repository property for every entity. The first checkout handler needs an order with its lines, so it calls

The belief: Clean Architecture requires wrapping EF Core in a generic repository and a unit of work. The Application layer must never see a
, and the wrapper is what makes it testable and lets you swap the ORM later.

The goals behind it are real. Business rules shouldn't depend on a persistence framework, and fast tests that don't need a database are valuable. Repository and Unit of Work are well-known patterns from Martin Fowler's catalog, Domain-Driven Design leans on repositories, and Microsoft's microservices guide uses them. Popular templates ship the generic version, so it looks like part of the architecture. The half-truth is that the goal is right and the generic shape is the problem.
EF Core's API reference says it directly:
is a combination of the Unit Of Work and Repository patterns. Fowler defines a repository as mediating between the domain and data mapping layers through a collection-like interface, which is what
collects changes and commits them together, which is
. Microsoft's guide notes that its own repositories rely on the
implementation of both patterns instead of duplicating it. A generic
class re-declares both, with fewer features.
The rule is about direction, not wrappers

content.text: Generic writes undo what the change tracker gives you
The change tracker knows which properties changed. A generic
throws that away. In a test with EF Core 10 on SQLite, it wrote every column of a loaded order back to the database, where saving through the change tracker sent only
. Given an entity built by hand with just
itself breaks the unit of work: an order saved by one repository stayed in the database when its line failed in the next.
Microsoft's guide describes the version that pays off: one repository per

, never one per table, with the interface in the domain layer and the implementation in infrastructure. Queries can go around it, as in CQRS, because they don't change state. The testing guide calls a repository layer the only approach that allows comprehensive, reliable stubbing of data access, at a significant cost, since every testable query becomes a method and still needs a test against the real database. The architecture guide is just as clear that repositories aren't mandatory.
The fix: name the queries, and let the context commit

content.text: This is our view, not a rule from the sources. For a small service or vertical-slice handlers, using the

directly is a legitimate choice, as long as it's decided and written down and the handlers have integration tests. For a domain with real invariants, use specific repositories on the write side and let reads project straight from the context. The generic repository with a unit-of-work class rarely earns its keep.
